newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar hits highest yen level in over four years.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits highest yen level in over four years.

text.p: The dollar jumped to its highest level against the yen in more than four years on Monday, buoyed by a possible increase in U.S. interest rates and supportive words last week from Washington's treasury secretary.
The dollar hit 125.00 yen in early afternoon trade in Tokyo, its highest level since February 2, 1993, when it traded at 125.25 yen.

The rise came even though Japan's current account figures for February, released on Monday morning, showed its trade surplus rising, something likely to stir up fresh trade friction with the United States.
The surplus in the current account, which measures trade in goods and services, rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) in February from a year ago.
A weaker yen is likely to worsen the trade imbalance since it makes Japanese exports even more competitive abroad.
"The market largely shrugged off the current account data and everyone is buying dollars," said a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo.
In other Japanese markets, export-orientated companies listed on the Tokyo stock market benefited from the dollar's rise. Japanese government bond futures were little changed.

Currency traders said that there was strong underlying demand for the dollar, especially after the release of U.S. employment data on Friday that pointed to a possible further rise in U.S. interest rates.

"More of the large Japanese accounts are thinking we could go above 125 yen now and that the high for this week could be from 125.50 to 126.50 yen," said Ken Landon, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Tokyo.
The buying was also sparked in part by remarks on Friday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who said on a visit to Tokyo last week that exchange rates should not be used as a trade tool.
Traders took the statement to mean that Washington still favoured a strong dollar. The U.S. currency has risen from a post-war low of just under 80 yen in the spring of 1995.

Investor demand was also boosted by the prospect of a widening gap between U.S. and Japanese interest rates. Friday's job figures showed U.S. wage costs rising, fuelling speculation that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again, dealers said.
Traders said there were rumours in the market that Japan's the Ministry of Finance had contacted life insurers, which are big investors, and suggested that they not buy dollars.

There were also market rumours that the Bank of Japan was checking the dollar/yen rate, sometimes a precursor to intervention by the central bank. But by midday, no yen buying by the bank had been detected.

The weaker yen boosted Tokyo stocks in the morning though the main Nikkei index of 225 leading shares had dipped into negative territory by early afternoon on selling of shares in the financial and construction sectors. At 0510 GMT the index was down 110.11 points at 17750.48.
Bond futures showed little reaction to the dollar or trade figures with the benchmark June contract down 0.02 at 126.85.
Traders said the market was focused on a raft of new bonds expected to hit the market this week in both the corporate and government sectors. ($1=125 yen)
